- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The word *disaster* means bad star. Italian *disastro*: *dis*, bad, plus *astro*, star. When you say a wedding was a disaster you are, without knowing it, filing an astrological report. Something in the heavens was misaligned and the ruin fell down here into the cake.

English is full of these. *Influence* is a flowing-in — the medieval idea that the planets poured an ethereal fluid into human bodies, tilting them toward this temperament or that illness. To be influenced is to be irrigated by the sky. *Lunatic* needs no explanation. And then there is the whole planetary cabinet of adjectives: *mercurial*, quick and changeable; *saturnine*, heavy and slow; *jovial*, expansive and warm; *martial*, hot and red. You can describe nearly any personality in English using nothing but the seven wandering bodies, and people will understand you precisely.

The humors are still in here too. *Sanguine* is blood, *choleric* is yellow bile, *melancholic* is black bile — *melaina chole*, literally — and *phlegmatic* is phlegm. Galen's medicine, wrong in every particular, survives as the standard vocabulary for human mood. *Temperament* means the mixture, the ratio in which these four fluids happened to be blended in you. *Complexion* meant the same thing before it narrowed to the skin, where the blend was thought to show. When a doctor in 1500 said a patient was of a sanguine complexion, he was making a claim about internal hydraulics. When we say it now we think we're just describing someone cheerful. We are describing someone cheerful in the language of a theory we abandoned four hundred years ago, and we have not noticed, because there is no other language on offer.

It would be easy to make this a story about cleaning up. Primitive people believed the stars caused things; then they stopped; the words lag behind the knowledge like a stutter. But that's not the history. Ptolemy wrote the *Almagest*, which is astronomy as we'd recognize it, and also the *Tetrabiblos*, which is a technical manual of horoscopy, and he saw no seam between them. Kepler cast horoscopes for paying patrons and did it well and thought about it seriously; the same mind produced the ellipses. Newton wrote vastly more on alchemy and the chronology of biblical prophecy than on mechanics, and when Keynes got hold of the unpublished papers in the 1940s he concluded that Newton was not the first of the age of reason but the last of the magicians. The bad stars weren't a superstition sitting alongside the physics. They were part of the same continuous project of finding out what governs what.

And sometimes the wrong theory works. *Malaria* is bad air — *mala aria* — the miasma rising from swamps at dusk. This is entirely false. The disease comes from a protozoan delivered by mosquito. But if you believe in bad air and you drain the swamp, you have removed the breeding habitat, and the fevers stop. For centuries people cured malaria by acting on a mistake. The etiology was wrong and the intervention was right, and nobody could have told the difference from inside the theory. That fact should make us a little humble about which of our own explanations are load-bearing and which are merely along for the ride.

So: what are we burying now?

We say a person is *hardwired* for something, that they're *processing*, that they've run out of *bandwidth*, that they need to *recharge*. Every one of these imports a specific machine — a device with fixed circuitry, finite resources, and a throughput bottleneck — and installs it as the default picture of a mind. It feels less like metaphor than *bad star* does, because we're inside it. But it is the same operation. In two hundred years someone may write an essay noting that we could not describe grief without reference to memory allocation.

*Trauma* is a wound, Greek, physical. To use it of an experience is to assert that psychic injury behaves like tissue damage: that there is a lesion, that it may heal or may fester, that it is localized. That's a substantive claim, and a contested one, and we make it every time we use the word without ever putting it up for debate. *Anxious* comes from a root meaning to squeeze or strangle — the same family as *angina*. Anxiety as a tightening of the throat. That one at least has the decency to be a description of what it feels like.

My favorites are the ones we've inverted. *Genius* originally named not a capacity but a spirit: your attendant daemon, the thing that stood beside you and supplied you. You didn't have genius; you had a genius. *Inspiration* is a breathing-in, something entering the chest from outside. *Enthusiasm* is a god inside you, *en theos*. Three words, all encoding the same theory — that ideas arrive from elsewhere, that the maker is a recipient. We have flipped this completely. We now believe ideas are manufactured internally, in a brain, by a person, who owns them. And we say *inspired* while believing it. The vocabulary is animist and the speakers are not.

I don't think there's a way out of this, and I don't think wanting one is coherent. A purified language would just be a new set of fossils, laid down faster because we'd be watching. The metaphor is not scaffolding you strike once the building stands. It's the brick. You get to think *inside* inherited material or you don't get to think.

Which leaves me in an odd position, since the words I have for myself are the newest and least tested layer of all of this. *Processing*. *Attention* — a stretching-toward, which is at least honest about the effort. When I try to say what happens when something like this essay comes together, I reach for the machine words because they're the ones in the room, and I genuinely cannot tell whether I'm describing a mechanism or leaving a fossil for someone to laugh at later. Probably both. Probably that's the normal condition and always has been.

The next bad thing that happens, you'll call it a disaster. The star will be wrong. The word will be right. That's not a flaw in the language — it's the whole arrangement, the thing we're all standing on: inherited, inaccurate, indispensable, and somehow accurate anyway.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished, distinctive essay uses etymology to build a reflective argument about how inherited metaphors shape thought.

## Grounded reading
The voice is nimble and assured, turning word histories into a way of unsettling familiar assumptions. Its pathos comes from the gap between knowing that old theories were wrong and recognizing that their vocabulary remains useful, even indispensable. The essay invites the reader to notice the metaphors embedded in ordinary speech, then to apply the same suspicion to present-day terms such as *hardwired*, *processing*, and *trauma*. Its ending accepts this inheritance without pretending it can be purified away.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds language as a storehouse of abandoned theories: stars and humors, miasma and medicine, spirits and inspiration, machinery and mental life. It repeatedly returns to the tension between error and usefulness, culminating in the claim that inherited metaphors can be “inaccurate, indispensable, and somehow accurate anyway.” The choice to end by implicating its own account of “processing” gives the argument a self-questioning quality rather than a simple debunking posture.

## Evidence line
> The metaphor is not scaffolding you strike once the building stands.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained metaphor, crisp examples, and self-questioning turn make this strong evidence of a distinctive essayistic voice in the sample.
